t:
(a) Sense of Congress.—It is the sense of Congress that—
        (1) the United States Government should expand efforts to peacefully address Venezuela’s humanitarian crisis; and 
        (2) humanitarian assistance—
            (A) should be targeted toward those most in need and delivered through partners that uphold internationally recognized humanitarian principles; and 
            (B) should not be passed through the control or distribution mechanisms of the Maduro regime.   
    (b) Humanitarian Relief.—
        (1) In general.—The Secretary of State, in coordination with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall provide—
            (A) humanitarian assistance to individuals and communities in Venezuela, including—
                (i) public health commodities and services, including medicines and basic medical supplies and equipment; 
                (ii) basic food commodities and nutritional supplements needed to address growing malnutrition and improve food security for the people of Venezuela, with a specific emphasis on the most vulnerable populations; and 
                (iii) technical assistance to ensure that health and food commodities are appropriately selected, procured, targeted, and distributed; and  
            (B) Venezuelans and hosting communities, as appropriate, in neighboring countries with humanitarian aid, such as—
                (i) urgently needed health and nutritional assistance, including logistical and technical assistance to hospitals and health centers in affected communities; 
                (ii) food assistance for vulnerable individuals, including assistance to improve food security for affected communities; and 
                (iii) hygiene supplies and sanitation services.   
        (2) Aid to venezuelans in neighboring countries.—The aid described in paragraph (1)(B)—
            (A) may be provided—
                (i) directly to Venezuelans in neighboring countries, including countries of the Caribbean; or 
                (ii) indirectly through the communities in which the Venezuelans reside; and  
            (B) should focus on the most vulnerable Venezuelans in neighboring countries.   
    (c) Humanitarian Assistance Strategy Update.—Not later than 180 days after the date of the enactment of this Act, the Secretary of State, in coordination with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall submit, to the appropriate congressional committees, an update to the Venezuela humanitarian assistance strategy described in the conference 
report accompanying the Consolidated Appropriations Act (Public Law 116–6), to cover a 2-year period and include—
        (1) a description of the United States humanitarian assistance provided under this section; 
        (2) a description of United States diplomatic efforts to ensure support from international donors, including regional partners in Latin America and the Caribbean, for the provision of humanitarian assistance to the people of Venezuela; 
        (3) the identification of governments that are willing to provide financial and technical assistance for the provision of such humanitarian assistance to the people of Venezuela and a description of such assistance; and 
        (4) the identification of the financial and technical assistance to be provided by multilateral institutions, including the United Nations humanitarian agencies, the Pan American Health Organization, the Inter-American Development Bank, and the World Bank, and a description of such assistance.  
    (d) Diplomatic Engagement.—The Secretary of State, in consultation with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall work with relevant foreign governments and multilateral organizations to coordinate a donors summit and carry out diplomatic engagement to advance the strategy required under subsection (c). 
    (e) Authorization of Appropriations.—There is authorized to be appropriated $400,000,000 for fiscal year 2020 to carry out the activities set forth in subsection (b). 
    (f) Defined Term.—In this section, the term “appropriate congressional committees” means—
        (1) the Committee on Foreign Relations of the Senate; 
        (2) the Committee on Appropriations of the Senate; 
        (3) the Committee on Foreign Affairs of the House of Representatives; and 
        (4) the Committee on Appropriations of the House of Representatives.

fable.w: The tempting reading is that working with foreign governments and multilateral organizations is coordination with outside parties. But this is diplomatic engagement to carry out an already-set strategy and organize a donors summit, not outside input into a federal decision. The other procedural elements are coordination between the Secretary of State and the USAID Administrator and a strategy update sent to congressional committees, all of which stay inside the federal government. There is no comment period, rulemaking, advisory body, or right to sue.
fable.s: shall work with relevant foreign governments and multilateral organizations to coordinate a donors summit and carry out diplomatic engagement to advance the strategy required under subsection (c)

opus.w: The tempting reading is that working with foreign governments and multilateral organizations counts as outside participation. But this is diplomacy to carry out a strategy already required by the section, not outsiders giving input before a federal decision. The other process language is State–USAID coordination, which stays inside the federal government, and a strategy report to congressional committees, which also stays inside. Delivering aid through partners is just how the aid is distributed and gives them no part in the decision.
opus.s: The Secretary of State, in consultation with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall work with relevant foreign governments and multilateral organizations to coordinate a donors summit and carry out diplomatic engagement to advance the strategy required under subsection (c).
opus.b:
Label: **No**. The tempting reading is subsection (d). The Secretary must "work with relevant foreign governments and multilateral organizations to coordinate a donors summit," and those are parties outside the federal government. But this is diplomacy to carry out a strategy that is already required. The outsiders are not being consulted before a federal decision is made.

The rest of the section stays inside the federal government:
- **State and USAID:** their "coordination" and "consultation" happens between two federal agencies.
- **Strategy update:** it is a report to congressional committees, which are inside the federal government.
- **Aid delivery:** handing out aid through "partners" is how the aid gets delivered. Those partners have no say in the decision.

My confidence is moderate (0.72), because subsection (d) could be read as coordinating with outside entities before a federal action.

qwen_chat.w: The section requires coordination between federal agencies (State and USAID), which is intra-governmental. While it mentions working with foreign governments, this is for diplomatic engagement and aid delivery, not for consulting outsiders on a federal decision-making process like rulemaking or permitting. The reports are submitted to Congress, which is inside the federal government.
qwen_chat.s: The Secretary of State, in consultation with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall work with relevant foreign governments and multilateral organizations to coordinate a donors summit
qwen_chat.b:
Tempting-but-wrong reading: One might argue that "coordination" with foreign governments or multilateral organizations constitutes participation because these entities are outside the U.S. federal government. However, the definition specifies that participation involves consulting or coordinating with people outside the government *before making a decision* in a way that brings them into the decision-making process (like an advisory board or public comment). Here, the coordination is for diplomatic engagement and aid delivery, which is an executive function, not a participatory decision-making mechanism involving outsiders in the regulatory or policy sense defined. More importantly, the primary interactions described are between federal agencies (State and USAID) or with Congress (reports). The "coordination" with foreign entities is for the *delivery* of aid, not for *consulting* them on a federal decision. The definition's examples (advisory boards, comment periods, hearings) do not fit this diplomatic coordination. Furthermore, the "consultation" mentioned in (d) is between the Secretary of State and the Administrator of USAID, which is intra-governmental.

Wait, let's re-read carefully.
(b)(1) "The Secretary of State, in coordination with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development..." -> Intra-governmental.
(c) "submit... to the appropriate congressional committees" -> Congress is inside.
(d) "The Secretary of State, in consultation with the Administrator of the United States Agency for International Development, shall work with relevant foreign governments and multilateral organizations to coordinate a donors summit..." -> The consultation is with USAID (inside). The working with foreign governments is for a summit. Is this "participation"? The definition says "Participation is when the federal government may or must consult or coordinate with people outside of the government before making a decision." Does coordinating a donors summit count as "making a decision" in the sense of the definition? Usually, "participation" in this legal labeling context refers to rulemaking, advisory committees, or specific decision-making processes where outsiders have a voice. Diplomatic coordination for aid delivery is generally considered executive action, not "participation" in the sense of public input or advisory input on a specific federal decision like a rule or permit. The definition emphasizes "advisory board, committee, or commission", "comment period", "public hearing". This section is about aid delivery and diplomatic strategy.

Let's look at the "No" traps: "consultation or coordination BETWEEN federal agencies... is not participation". The consultation in (d) is between State and USAID. The coordination with foreign governments is for a summit. This is not a decision-making process where the foreign governments are consulted *before* a federal decision is made in the regulatory/policy sense. It's an operational/diplomatic activity.

Therefore, the label is No.
